## Purpose

The purpose of this assignment is to develop and evaluate publication-quality visualizations of results from the final project, emphasizing the presentation of underlying data, statistical uncertainty, and clear interpretation in a Click-to-Run file that can be rendered as HTML and PDF across various operating systems (e.g., Mac, Windows, Linux).

### Core: Task 1

*Choose one result from your project pipeline that the final report depends on; typically the Step-5 regression-effects figure or the Step-1 power curves, though any figure the report requires qualifies. Say in a sentence or two why this is the one you are drafting first.*

The figure selected for this assignment will present the statistical power results from Step 1 of the final project, examining how the probability of detecting small and medium regression effects changes across sample sizes. This figure is being developed first because identifying the sample sizes needed to achieve adequate statistical power is a central objective of the simulation study, and the power curves will communicate these findings more directly than a numerical table alone.

### Core: Task 2

*Produce exactly one figure of that result, generated by code in the click-to-run document that pulls from your actual project pipeline, either by reading your simulation’s stored results, re-running a scoped-down version, or reading your project’s data. Hand- typed numbers, pasted screenshots, and toy stand-in data are not acceptable outputs to visualize.*

```{r}

# Load regression function from Assignment 04
source("R/regression_functions.R")

# Load package
library(dplyr)

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(20261117)

# Define simulation conditions
sample_sizes <- c(50, 100, 200, 400, 600, 1000)
effect_sizes <- c(0, 0.1, 0.3)

condition_grid <- expand.grid(
  n = sample_sizes,
  beta1 = effect_sizes
)

# Define simulation parameters
beta0 <- 2
beta2 <- 0.4
sigma <- 1
alpha <- 0.05
n_replications <- 400

# Store individual replication results
simulation_results <- vector(
  "list",
  nrow(condition_grid) * n_replications
)

result_index <- 1

# Run simulation
for (condition in seq_len(nrow(condition_grid))) {
  
  n <- condition_grid$n[condition]
  beta1 <- condition_grid$beta1[condition]
  
  for (rep in seq_len(n_replications)) {
    
    # Generate predictors
    X <- cbind(
      x1 = rnorm(n),
      x2 = rnorm(n)
    )
    
    # Generate outcome
    y <- beta0 +
      beta1 * X[, "x1"] +
      beta2 * X[, "x2"] +
      rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sigma)
    
    # Fit regression using Assignment 04 function
    model <- fit_matrix_reg(y, X)
    
    # Extract results for coefficient of interest
    beta_hat <- model$coefficients[2, 1]
    analytical_se <- model$standard_errors[2]
    p_value <- model$p_values[2]
    
    # Store replication-level results
    simulation_results[[result_index]] <- data.frame(
      n = n,
      beta1 = beta1,
      replication = rep,
      estimate = beta_hat,
      standard_error = analytical_se,
      p_value = p_value,
      significant = p_value < alpha
    )
    
    result_index <- result_index + 1
  }
}

# Combine replication-level results
simulation_results <- bind_rows(simulation_results)

# Calculate rejection rates and Monte Carlo uncertainty
power_results <- simulation_results %>%
  group_by(n, beta1) %>%
  summarise(
    replications = n(),
    rejection_rate = mean(significant),
    mcse = sqrt(
      rejection_rate * (1 - rejection_rate) / replications
    ),
    lower = pmax(0, rejection_rate - 1.96 * mcse),
    upper = pmin(1, rejection_rate + 1.96 * mcse),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Display simulation summary
print(as.data.frame(power_results), row.names = FALSE)

```

The simulation results provide estimated rejection rates and associated Monte Carlo uncertainty across the specified sample sizes and effect sizes. Under the null-effect condition ($\beta_1 = 0$), the rejection rate represents the false-positive rate, whereas under the nonzero-effect conditions ($\beta_1 = 0.1$ and $\beta_1 = 0.3$), it represents statistical power. The following figure focuses on the nonzero-effect conditions to illustrate how statistical power changes with sample size and effect magnitude. The estimated power values are accompanied by approximate 95% Monte Carlo uncertainty intervals, with a reference line indicating the target of 80% power.

```{r}

# Load visualization package
library(ggplot2)

# Retain nonzero effect conditions for power curves
power_plot_data <- power_results %>%
  filter(beta1 != 0) %>%
  mutate(
    effect = factor(
      beta1,
      levels = sort(unique(beta1)),
      labels = paste0(
        "Effect size = ",
        sort(unique(beta1))
      )
    )
  )

# Create statistical power curves
power_figure <- ggplot(
  power_plot_data,
  aes(
    x = n,
    y = rejection_rate,
    color = effect,
    fill = effect,
    group = effect
  )
) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    alpha = 0.15,
    color = NA
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0.80,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = sort(unique(power_plot_data$n))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Power Across Sample Sizes",
    subtitle = "Two-predictor linear regression simulation",
    x = "Sample size (n)",
    y = "Estimated statistical power",
    color = "True effect size",
    fill = "True effect size"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

# Display figure
print(power_figure)

```

### Core: Task 3

*The figure must meet the class checklist: it shows the underlying data or simulation results (not only summaries of them); it encodes uncertainty; its axes are reasonable and clear; and its labels make it readable without the caption.*

The figure displays the estimated rejection rates from the simulation across the evaluated sample sizes and nonzero effect sizes, with each plotted point representing the proportion of statistically significant results across 400 replications. The shaded bands represent approximate 95% Monte Carlo uncertainty intervals, allowing readers to assess the precision of the power estimates. The sample-size axis uses the evaluated numerical values, while the power axis spans 0 to 1 to avoid exaggerating differences between conditions. The title, axis labels, and legend identify the simulation context and distinguish the two effect sizes, and the dashed horizontal line provides a reference for the conventional 80% power threshold. Together, these features communicate the observed simulation results and their uncertainty without relying solely on a fitted trend or numerical summary.

### Core: Task 4

*Write a caption (2–4 sentences) that states the takeaway (e.g., what the reader should conclude) rather than describing the mechanics of the plot. “Higher X predicts higher Y, with substantial unexplained variation” is a caption; “scatterplot of Y versus X with fitted line” is a description.*

Statistical power increased with sample size for both effect sizes, although substantially larger samples were needed to detect the smaller effect. For the medium effect (β₁ = 0.3), estimated power exceeded 80% at n = 100 (82.75%), whereas the small effect (β₁ = 0.1) did not exceed this threshold until n = 1,000 (86.75%) among the sample sizes evaluated. The shaded intervals represent Monte Carlo uncertainty based on 400 simulation replications per condition, highlighting the precision of the estimated power values.

### Stretch: Task 1

*Your submission must additionally present the same result in a genuinely different visualization form, a different geometry or encoding, not the same plot restyled with new colors and a nicer theme, and a short argued verdict (5–8 sentences) on which of the two belongs in the final report. Your argument must be grounded in the visualization principles from class: what each form makes easy or hard to see, and for which audience. The goal here is to create a plausible alternative and think deeply about why one might be better or worse (and maybe it’s different audiences or situations that determines which you would choose).*

As an alternative to the power curves, the same simulation results are presented using a faceted dot-and-interval plot. This visualization displays the estimated statistical power and associated Monte Carlo uncertainty for each sample size, with separate panels for the small and medium effect sizes. Rather than emphasizing changes in power across sample sizes through connected lines, this representation highlights individual simulation conditions and their relationship to the 80% power threshold.

```{r}

# Create alternative dot-and-interval visualization
alternative_figure <- ggplot(
  power_plot_data,
  aes(
    x = rejection_rate,
    y = factor(n),
    color = effect
  )
) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0.80,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  geom_errorbarh(
    aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper),
    height = 0.2,
    linewidth = 0.7,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 2.5,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ effect, ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Estimated Statistical Power by Sample Size",
    subtitle = "Points and approximate 95% Monte Carlo intervals",
    x = "Estimated statistical power",
    y = "Sample size (n)",
    color = "True effect size"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

# Display alternative figure
print(alternative_figure)

```

Both visualizations communicate the relationship between sample size, effect magnitude, and statistical power, but they emphasize different aspects of the simulation results. The power curves make it easier to identify how power increases with sample size and to compare the trajectories of small and medium effects. In contrast, the dot-and-interval plot emphasizes the individual power estimates and their Monte Carlo uncertainty, making it easier to assess whether particular simulation conditions reach the 80% power threshold. The alternative also separates the effect sizes into panels, reducing overlap but making direct comparisons between them somewhat less immediate. For readers primarily interested in the precision of individual estimates, such as researchers evaluating specific sample-size choices, the dot-and-interval plot may be more useful. However, for a broader research audience, the power curves provide a more intuitive representation of the relationship between sample size and statistical power. I would therefore select the power curves for the final report because they communicate the central finding more directly while still displaying the uncertainty associated with the simulation estimates.
